I should just pack a meal, but so far I've been buying something to eat between PT and the class. So it is that for the first time in years I've stepped foot in the sorts of restaurants that now serve as Bastions of Lord Beetus. Last week, while waiting for my meal inside a Five Guys, I saw more fats than I usually do in an entire day.

The first one greeted me from behind the counter. It's been years since I've been to a Five Guys, so I was asking about the menu to make sure I ordered correctly. The fat had the impression that I'd never set foot in a Five Guys, and took on the air of a hipster sharing the details of a club whose entrance was unmarked and hidden in an alley.

Me: "How large are the small (i think they might have even called them "tiny") fries?"

It (smugly): "About the size of a McDonalds Medium."

Me: "Okay, I'll have a burger -- "

It: "What kind of burger?"

Me: "Just a regular hamburger...(this was an option, I think it just assumed nobody would order it. Is "burger" really that ambiguous?)"

I ordered toppings, too, and declined a milkshake. You get the idea. My order was delayed, so I got some great people-watching in. Aside from a single human employee and myself, I didn't see anyone in the restaurant who wasn't obese. When my order came up twenty minutes later, I discovered that someone at the restaurant had added a patty to my modest burger and dumped an additional couple small orders worth of fries into the bag. I think it was supposed to be in apology.

It was kind of a nice gesture (props to the chain's human founder, who I read up on while eating, for motivating his hammy employees to appease their fat clientele), and was fine by me because I was basically making up for two meals that day. But my extra food also got me thinking about the underlying psychology of it. I'm sure the fatties all love the generous fries (in fact, "extra fries in the bag" was one of the things that the morbidly obese guy who first convinced me to go to Five Guys a few years ago highlighted as a selling point of the restaurant).

But what if I didn't want or couldn't afford to eat all that food?

I'd either be forced to eat cold, greasy fries (which I still wound up doing later that night because it was too much food for one sitting) and/or a cold/soggy burger, or binge eat the whole mess, or throw out food. We all know what most Americans are going to do.

So now I'm wondering if my experience at Five Guys was unique. Is Five Guys the only restaurant packaging binge eating as normal, or even as a reward? I doubt it.
